name: The Underground Railroad
place: Southern United States to the North, Canada, and Mexico
intro: The Underground Railroad was a secret network of people and hiding places. It helped enslaved people escape from the South to freedom in the North, Canada, and other places. Freedom seekers and their helpers showed great courage, because escaping and helping were both against the law.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: About 1810 to 1865, busiest in the 1850s

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: From the Southern states to free states, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Enslaved African Americans seeking freedom

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: Possibly more than 100,000 people; no one knows the exact number

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Mostly the Northern free states and Canada

timeline.text: Pennsylvania becomes the first state to pass a law to end slavery.
Harriet Tubman escapes slavery in Maryland.
The Fugitive Slave Act makes the North unsafe, so many freedom seekers go on to Canada.
Harriet Tubman helps lead a raid that frees more than 700 enslaved people.
The Civil War ends, and slavery ends in the United States.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: Before the Civil War, slavery was legal in the Southern United States. The Underground Railroad was not a real railroad, and it did not run under the ground. It was a secret network of people, homes, and hiding places. It helped enslaved people escape to freedom from about 1810 until the 1860s.

People used railroad words as a secret code. Guides who led people were called conductors. Hiding places, such as homes and barns, were called stations or depots. Helping freedom seekers was against the law, so everything had to stay secret.

Many kinds of people helped. Free Black people and formerly enslaved people, like Harriet Tubman, were some of the bravest conductors. Quakers and other people who were against slavery opened their homes, too. The National Park Service calls the people who escaped "freedom seekers."

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Enslaved people did not have freedom. They could be sold away from their families at any time. Harriet Tubman escaped in 1849 when her enslaver died and she was going to be sold. Many people decided to risk everything to be free.

Running away was very dangerous. Slave catchers watched the roads and rivers that freedom seekers were likely to use. Enslavers also offered rewards to people who caught them. A reward of one hundred dollars was offered for Harriet Tubman.

In 1850, the United States passed the Fugitive Slave Act. This law said that freedom seekers found in free states must be sent back to their enslavers. After this law, even the Northern states were not safe. Many freedom seekers had to travel all the way to Canada.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Most freedom seekers traveled north toward the free states and Canada. Many walked at night and hid during the day. Stations were usually about 10 to 20 miles apart. People rested in basements, barns, churches, or caves.

Some people used the stars to find north. Others rode in wagons, sometimes hidden under hay. Some escaped by boat along rivers and the Atlantic Coast, often with help from Black sailors. Many freedom seekers in Texas went south to Mexico, where slavery was against the law.

Harriet Tubman made about 13 trips back to Maryland to rescue family and friends. She also gave directions to about 70 more people who escaped on their own. She later said she never lost a passenger. People called her "Moses."

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Between 1850 and 1860, about 30,000 to 40,000 freedom seekers settled in Canada. Most made new homes in Ontario, and some built whole villages. In Canada, Black people could live freely, serve on juries, and run for office. Still, they sometimes faced unfair treatment and had trouble finding jobs.

When the Civil War began, many freedom seekers joined the Union army. Harriet Tubman worked for the army as a nurse, scout, and spy. After the war, thousands of people returned to the South to find their families.

Today, people remember the Underground Railroad at museums and historic sites. The Levi Coffin House in Indiana was a station where freedom seekers hid. William Still of Philadelphia kept careful records of the people he helped. His 1872 book helps historians tell their stories today.

vocab.meaning: Forced to work for someone else without freedom or pay.
A person who escaped from slavery to find freedom.
A person who worked to end slavery.
On the Underground Railroad, a guide who led freedom seekers to safety.
A group of people and places that are connected and work together.

name: Native American Boarding Schools
place: Across the United States (first off-reservation school: Carlisle, Pennsylvania)
intro: For about 150 years, the U.S. government ran or paid for boarding schools for Native American children. Many children were taken from their families, often by force, and sent to schools far from home. At the schools, they were made to give up their languages, names, and cultures.

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: More than 400 schools in 37 states or territories, including Alaska and Hawaii

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: American Indian, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian children

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: Tens of thousands of children, according to federal records

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Boarding schools, often far from their families, such as Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania

timeline.text: Congress begins paying for schools to teach Native children.
Carlisle Indian Industrial School opens in Pennsylvania as the first off-reservation boarding school.
A new law lets federal officers take Native children from their homes to send them to school.
A government report finds that children at the schools are overworked and underfed.
The Indian Child Welfare Act gives Native parents the right to refuse to send their children to boarding schools.
The President apologizes for the boarding schools, and Carlisle becomes a national monument.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: From 1819 to 1969, the U.S. government ran or paid for boarding schools for Native children. A boarding school is a school where students live, eat, and sleep, away from their families. There were more than 400 of these schools in 37 states or territories. Some were in Alaska and Hawaii.

In 1879, an Army officer named Richard Pratt opened the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania. It was the first boarding school for Native children that was far away from their reservations. About 7,800 children from more than 140 Native nations went there before it closed in 1918. Carlisle became a model for hundreds of other schools.
Thousands of Native children were taken from their families, often by force. Some were only four or five years old. Federal records show that tens of thousands of children went to these schools.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: The government wanted Native children to give up their own ways of life and live like white Americans. This is called assimilation. Leaders believed it would be easier to change children if they were taken far away from their families and communities. The government also wanted to take more Native land.

Many families did not want to send their children away. In 1891, a law let federal officers take children from their homes. Some parents who refused to send their children were punished. For example, in 1895, 19 Hopi men were sent to prison on Alcatraz Island for refusing to send their children to school.
So, most children did not choose to go. Their families and nations did not choose it either. The government made the decision for them.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Children were sent to schools on or near reservations, or to schools far from home like Carlisle. Carlisle brought children from Native nations all over the country to Pennsylvania.

When children arrived, the schools tried to erase who they were. Staff cut the children's long hair and took away their traditional clothing. Children had to wear uniforms and were given new English names. They were not allowed to speak their Native languages, and they were punished if they did.

Life at the schools was strict, like the Army. Students marched in lines and spent much of their time doing hard work, not just schoolwork. A government report in 1928 found that children were overworked and did not get enough food. Many children got sick, and federal records show that nearly 1,000 children died while at the schools.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: The boarding schools separated children from their families, languages, and cultures. Many children grew up without learning their nation's language or traditions. The schools left lasting effects on survivors and on their children and grandchildren.

Over time, the laws changed. Most off-reservation boarding schools closed by the 1930s. In 1975, a new law let Native nations run their own education programs. In 1978, the Indian Child Welfare Act gave Native parents the right to say no to sending their children to boarding schools.

In 2022, the U.S. Department of the Interior released a report about the schools. Survivors shared their stories on a tour called the Road to Healing. In October 2024, President Joe Biden formally apologized for the boarding schools. In December 2024, the Carlisle school grounds became a national monument. Today, many Native nations are working to bring back their languages and traditions.

vocab.meaning: A school where students live and sleep, away from their families.
Forcing or expecting a group of people to give up their own culture and take on another one.
The language, beliefs, customs, food, and art of a group of people.
Land set aside by the U.S. government for a Native American nation.
A person who lived through something very hard.
Saying that you are sorry for something wrong that you did.

name: Trail of Tears
place: Southeastern United States to Indian Territory (Oklahoma)
intro: The Trail of Tears was the forced removal of Native American nations from their homelands in the Southeast. After Congress passed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, the U.S. government made about 100,000 Native people move west to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma. The Cherokee Nation's removal in 1838 and 1839 is the best-known part of this story, and thousands of Cherokee people died on the journey.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: 1830–1850 (Cherokee removal: 1838–1839)

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: From Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, North Carolina, and nearby lands to Indian Territory (Oklahoma)

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Seminole people

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 100,000 Native people were forced to move west

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma

timeline.text: Congress passes the Indian Removal Act.
The Choctaw Nation becomes the first nation forced to move west.
A small group of Cherokee people, not the nation's elected leaders, signs the Treaty of New Echota.
U.S. soldiers force Cherokee families into camps and send them west.
The last Cherokee groups reach Indian Territory, and John Ross is elected Principal Chief.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: In the early 1800s, five Native nations lived in the southeastern United States. They were the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw, and Seminole nations. White settlers wanted their land for farms, and some leaders wanted the United States to grow. In 1830, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, and President Andrew Jackson supported it.

The law was used to push Native nations west of the Mississippi River. Between 1830 and 1850, about 100,000 Native people were forced to leave their homes. The Choctaw were the first to go, starting in 1831. The Cherokee were the last, in 1838 and 1839.

This forced journey became known as the Trail of Tears. Today, people use that name for the removal of all five nations. Historians estimate that about 4,000 Cherokee people died before, during, or after the march.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: The Native nations did not want to leave. The Cherokee Nation had its own written language, created by Sequoyah, and its own written constitution. When gold was found on Cherokee land, the state of Georgia gave Cherokee land to white settlers. The Cherokee took their case to the U.S. Supreme Court and won, but the government still did not protect them.

In 1835, a small group of Cherokee people signed the Treaty of New Echota. None of them were elected leaders of the Cherokee Nation. The treaty traded all Cherokee land in the East for $5 million and land in Indian Territory. More than 15,000 Cherokee people protested the treaty, but the U.S. Senate approved it by just one vote.
The treaty gave the Cherokee two years to leave. By May 1838, only a few thousand had gone. The government then sent about 7,000 soldiers to force the rest of the Cherokee people out of their homes.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: In May 1838, soldiers rounded up Cherokee families and held them in crowded camps called stockades. Many families had to leave their homes and belongings behind. In the summer, a few groups traveled west by boat on rivers. Low water and hot, dry weather made that trip very hard.

Most Cherokee people waited in the camps until fall. Then about 12 groups of around 1,000 people each set out over land. They traveled on foot, on horseback, and in wagons, and some went by steamboat. Depending on the route, the trip was about 800 to 1,200 miles long.

The groups faced heavy rain, muddy roads, freezing weather, and too little food. Many people got sick, and many died from disease. By March 1839, all of the survivors had reached Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: The removal took the Cherokee people far from the land where their families had lived for generations. Thousands of people lost loved ones on the way. Later, some of the land promised to the nations in Indian Territory was taken from them too.

The Cherokee people worked hard to rebuild. In 1839, they elected John Ross as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. Tahlequah, Oklahoma, became their capital, and it is still the nation's headquarters today. About 1,000 Cherokee people stayed in the mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee. Their descendants are the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

Today, the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail crosses parts of nine states. The National Park Service says the trail helps people remember the removal and honor the survival of the Cherokee people.

A written agreement between nations or governments.

name: The Irish Potato Famine
intro: In 1845, a plant disease called blight began destroying Ireland's potato crops. Potatoes were the main food for poor families, so millions of people went hungry and about 1 million died. About 2 million people left Ireland, and most of them sailed to the United States.

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Ireland

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Mostly poor Irish farm families

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 2 million people left Ireland between 1845 and 1855

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Mostly the United States; also Canada, Great Britain, and Australia

timeline.text: Potato blight reaches Ireland, and potatoes begin to rot after the harvest.
Blight destroys most of Ireland's potato crop.
"Black '47" is the worst year. The Choctaw Nation sends $170 to help Irish families.
Ireland's census counts more than 1.5 million fewer people than in 1841.
Potato crops finally recover, and the famine is considered over.
John F. Kennedy, great-grandson of a famine immigrant, is elected U.S. president.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: In the 1840s, most poor families in Ireland depended on potatoes for food. More than half of the people relied on potatoes as their main food. Many families ate almost nothing else. Farmers grew mostly one kind of potato, called the Irish Lumper.
In 1845, a plant disease called blight reached Ireland. It made potatoes rot after the harvest. In 1846, the blight destroyed almost the whole potato crop. It kept coming back until about 1852.

More than three million people depended completely on potatoes, so huge numbers of families went hungry. About 1 million people died from hunger and sickness. The year 1847 was so bad that people called it "Black '47." In Irish, the famine is called An Gorta Mór, which means "the Great Hunger."

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Most Irish farmers were tenants who rented their land from rich landowners. Without potatoes, they had no food and very little money. Some landlords evicted families from their homes. Some even paid for ship tickets to send poor tenants away.

Ireland was ruled by Great Britain at the time. The British government bought corn from America to help, but it was not nearly enough. Meanwhile, food such as butter and livestock was still shipped out of Ireland. Many Irish people were angry that food left the country while people starved.

Families left to escape hunger and sickness and to find work. Between 1845 and 1855, more than 2 million people left Ireland. It was one of the largest movements of people from a single island in history.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Most emigrants sailed across the Atlantic Ocean to the United States. Others went to Canada, Great Britain, or Australia. So many went to Liverpool, England, that it was called "Ireland's second capital." Many people who landed in Canada later traveled south into the United States.

The ocean trip took about 40 days. Many ships were old cargo ships that were crowded and dirty. Passengers had little food or clean water, and sickness spread quickly. Because so many passengers became sick and died, people called these ships "coffin ships."

Most Irish immigrants settled in Boston, New York, and other cities on the East Coast. Many were too poor to travel any farther than the docks. They lived in crowded buildings near the ports, often in basements and attics. Families formed close Catholic communities to help each other.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Life in America was hard at first. Irish men took dangerous, low-paying jobs, like digging canals and laying railroad track. Women often worked as servants or in textile mills. Some job ads even said, "No Irish need apply."

Some Americans treated Irish immigrants unfairly because they were poor and Catholic. A political group called the Know-Nothings tried to keep immigrants out of power. Over time, though, Irish Americans became leaders in their cities. In 1960, John F. Kennedy, the great-grandson of a famine immigrant, was elected president.

The famine changed Ireland forever. Its population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.6 million in 1851. Today, about 32 million Americans have mostly Irish roots. Memorials in Ireland, New York City, Boston, and other places help people remember the Great Hunger.

name: The California Gold Rush
intro: In January 1848, a worker found gold at Sutter's Mill in California. Over the next few years, about 300,000 people rushed to California from across the United States and from many other countries, hoping to get rich. The Gold Rush helped California grow fast, but it brought terrible harm to the Native peoples who already lived there.

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Sutter's Mill near Coloma and the gold fields of Northern California

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Gold seekers called Forty-niners, mostly young men, from the U.S., Mexico, Chile, Peru, China, Hawaii, Europe, and Australia

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 300,000 people came to California

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Gold fields along California's rivers, and fast-growing towns like San Francisco and Sacramento

timeline.text: On January 24, James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill near Coloma, California.
On February 2, a treaty ended the Mexican-American War and gave California to the United States.
About 90,000 gold seekers, called Forty-niners, arrived in California.
California became the 31st state in September.
San Francisco grew to about 36,000 people, up from about 200 in 1846.
Only about 30,000 Native people were left in California, down from about 150,000 before the Gold Rush.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: On January 24, 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for John Sutter near Coloma, California. He spotted shiny flakes of gold in the river. Marshall and Sutter tried to keep the discovery a secret. But the news spread quickly, and soon people everywhere were talking about California gold.

That same year, a treaty ended the Mexican-American War, and California became part of the United States. At the time, only about 14,000 people who were not Native American lived in California. About 150,000 Native people also lived there, in many different nations. California had more kinds of Native peoples than any other part of North America.
The Gold Rush lasted from 1848 to about 1855. A few people became very rich, but most did not. When the gold in an area ran out, miners moved on, and some busy towns became empty ghost towns.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: People moved to California for one big reason: the chance to find gold and get rich. Stories about gold lying in the rivers spread around the world. Many people hoped to dig up a fortune and return home wealthy. These gold seekers were called Forty-niners, because so many arrived in 1849.

The gold seekers came from many countries. In 1848, the first miners came from Hawaii, Oregon, Mexico, Chile, Peru, and China. People from Europe and Australia soon followed. By 1849, about two-thirds of the newcomers were from the United States, and the rest came from other countries.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: About 6,000 newcomers arrived in 1848, and about 90,000 more came in 1849. In all, about 300,000 people came to California during the Gold Rush. About half of them traveled by sea on ships. The other half came over land, often on the California Trail.

Most gold seekers headed to the rivers and hills of Northern California, near the Sierra Nevada mountains. They set up mining camps and washed dirt from the rivers to find gold. New towns grew very fast. San Francisco grew from about 200 people in 1846 to about 36,000 people in 1852.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: The Gold Rush changed California quickly. So many people arrived that California became the 31st state in 1850, only about two years after gold was found. People from many countries now lived and worked side by side. Store owners who sold supplies to miners often earned more money than the miners did.

For California's Native peoples, the Gold Rush was a disaster. Gold was first found on the land of the Nisenan people. Miners took over Native lands and polluted the rivers, which killed fish and left less food to eat. Some newcomers attacked Native villages and killed many people. A California law passed in 1850 even allowed some Native people, including children, to be forced to work for settlers.

Sickness, hunger, and violence caused the deaths of about 120,000 Native people during the Gold Rush years. By 1870, only about 30,000 Native people were left in California, and most had been forced onto reservations. Today, California Native nations are still here. They work to protect their lands, languages, and cultures, and to make sure this history is remembered.

name: The Dust Bowl
intro: In the 1930s, a long drought and huge dust storms struck the southern Great Plains. Farmers could not grow crops, and the Great Depression made life even harder. About 2.5 million people left the Plains states, and many traveled west to California.

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Farm families and other people from the Plains

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 2.5 million people left the Plains states by 1940

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Nearby towns and states, and west to California

timeline.text: A long drought begins on the Plains.
Dust storms begin to blow across the dry farmland.
A huge storm carries dust all the way to Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C.
On April 14, the Black Sunday storm turns day into night. Congress passes a law to protect the soil.
Rain returns, and the long drought ends in most of the region.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: In the 1930s, a terrible drought hit the Great Plains of the United States. The worst area was centered on the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma. It also included parts of Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico. This area became known as the Dust Bowl.

Before the drought, farmers had plowed up millions of acres of grassland to grow wheat. The roots of the native grasses had held the soil in place. When the rain stopped, the bare soil dried out and turned to dust. Strong winds picked it up and blew it away.

Huge dust storms called "black blizzards" rolled across the land. The worst one came on April 14, 1935, a day called Black Sunday. The dust was so thick that people could not see their own hands in front of their faces. Some storms carried dust all the way to the East Coast.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Farm families could not grow crops in the blowing dust. Dust piled up against houses, and many farm animals died. People spent hours cleaning dust out of their homes. Some farmers tied clotheslines between the house and the barn so they could find their way in a storm.

At the same time, the Great Depression made money very hard to find. Wheat prices had fallen, so farmers earned very little. By 1935, more than 500,000 Americans had lost their homes. Often, banks took their land.
Many families felt they had no choice but to leave. About one in four people on the Plains moved away. Still, about three out of four farmers stayed on their land and kept trying.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: By 1940, about 2.5 million people had left the Plains states. Many moved only to nearby towns or counties that were less damaged. Others traveled far to the west. About 200,000 of them moved to California.

Families packed everything they owned into old cars and trucks called "jalopies." Many drove west on Route 66, a famous highway. They had heard there were farm jobs in California. Many came from Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri, Kansas, and Texas.

In California, many families worked in the fields picking grapes and cotton. They were paid very little for long, hard days. Many lived in tents or small shacks without plumbing or electricity. The government built camps for some families, where people helped run their own communities.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Many Californians did not welcome the newcomers. They called the migrants "Okies," no matter which state they came from. Migrants faced discrimination when they looked for work. The Los Angeles police chief even sent officers to the state border to turn poor families away.

The government also worked to heal the land. In 1935, Congress passed a law to help protect the soil. Farmers learned better ways to plow and plant. Between 1934 and 1942, the government planted about 220 million trees as windbreaks to slow the wind.

Rain finally returned in 1939, and much of the land recovered by the early 1940s. Some migrants went home, but many stayed in their new states. Over time, families replaced their shacks with real houses and became part of their communities. Photographer Dorothea Lange took pictures that helped Americans understand their struggle.

name: Japanese American Incarceration
intro: During World War II, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 Japanese Americans to leave their homes on the West Coast. Families were sent to prison camps in remote places, even though most of them were American citizens and none had done anything wrong. This event is often called Japanese internment, but many historians now call it Japanese American incarceration.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: 1942–1946, during World War II

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: From California, Oregon, and Washington to 10 camps in the western states and Arkansas

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Japanese immigrants and their American-born children and grandchildren

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 120,000 people; about two out of three were U.S. citizens

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Camps such as Manzanar (California), Heart Mountain (Wyoming), and Rohwer (Arkansas)

timeline.text: On December 7, Japan bombs Pearl Harbor, and the United States enters World War II.
In February, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signs Executive Order 9066.
Japanese American families are sent to temporary centers, then to 10 camps.
The government announces it will stop holding Japanese Americans in camps.
President Ronald Reagan signs the Civil Liberties Act, which apologizes and pays survivors $20,000 each.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: Japanese immigrants began coming to the United States to work in the 1880s. Many settled on the West Coast, where they started farms, stores, and other businesses. Their children were born in the United States, so they were American citizens. Even so, Japanese Americans often faced unfair treatment because of their race.

On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The United States entered World War II. In February 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. The order let the Army remove people from areas on the West Coast, and it was used against Japanese Americans.

About 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forced to leave their homes. About two out of three of them were U.S. citizens. Whole families, including children, were sent away. They were held in camps for most of the war.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Japanese Americans did not choose to move. The government ordered them to leave, and the Army carried out the orders. Leaders said it was a "military necessity" to keep the country safe during the war.

Years later, a group set up by Congress studied what happened. It found that the reason the government gave was false. Japanese Americans had not been a danger to the country. Prejudice against people of Japanese ancestry was a big part of why they were sent away.

A few Japanese Americans challenged the orders in court. Fred Korematsu refused to leave his home and took his case to the U.S. Supreme Court. The court sided with the government. Most families obeyed the orders, even though they knew the orders were unfair.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Families sometimes had only 48 hours to get ready to leave. They could bring only what they could carry. Many had to sell or leave behind their homes, farms, businesses, and belongings.

First, people went to temporary centers for a few weeks or months. Then they were moved to one of 10 camps in remote places. The camps were in California, Arizona, Idaho, Utah, Wyoming, Colorado, and Arkansas. Manzanar, in the California desert, is one of the best-known camps.

The camps were crowded and surrounded by barbed wire, with guards in watchtowers. Families lived in crowded barracks. Even so, people worked to make life as normal as they could. Children went to school, and camps had bands, sports teams, and baseball games.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Many Japanese Americans lost their homes, farms, and businesses while they were away. When people left the camps, each person was given $25 and a ticket home. Many families had to start over with almost nothing.

Some young Japanese American men joined the Army during the war. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, made up mostly of Japanese Americans, fought bravely in Europe. Many of their families were still living in the camps.

Starting in the 1970s, Japanese Americans worked to get the government to admit it was wrong. In 1988, President Ronald Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act. The law apologized and gave $20,000 to each survivor. Today, Manzanar is a National Historic Site, and people gather there every year to remember.

vocab.meaning: Being locked up or held in a prison or camp.
Holding people in camps during a war, often without a trial. Many people call this event Japanese internment.
A rule given by the President that the government must follow.
The family members and countries a person's family came from long ago.

name: Silicon Valley
place: San Francisco Bay Area, California, United States
intro: Silicon Valley is the southern part of the San Francisco Bay Area, where many computer and technology companies began. Starting in the mid-1900s, scientists, engineers, and workers moved there from across the United States and around the world for new technology jobs. People are still moving there today, and the area has grown to about 3 million people.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: From the 1950s to today

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Santa Clara Valley and the southern San Francisco Bay Area, including San Jose, Palo Alto, Mountain View, and Sunnyvale

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Scientists, engineers, and workers from across the U.S. and the world, especially East and South Asia

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 3.1 million people lived in Silicon Valley in 2020; in 1999, about one-third of its scientists and engineers were immigrants

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Cities and towns of the Santa Clara Valley, where orchards were replaced by technology companies

timeline.text: Two Stanford graduates started Hewlett-Packard in a garage in Palo Alto.
Stanford Industrial Park opened for new technology companies.
Lockheed opened in Sunnyvale and soon had 28,000 workers, the most in the area.
Eight engineers started Fairchild Semiconductor, a company that made computer parts from silicon.
A news writer made the name "Silicon Valley" popular.
About 3.1 million people lived in Silicon Valley.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: For thousands of years, the Ohlone people lived in the valley south of San Francisco Bay. Much later, the Santa Clara Valley became famous for its fruit orchards. Until the 1960s, it was the largest fruit-growing area in the world. People called it "the Valley of Heart's Delight."

In 1939, two Stanford University graduates started a company called Hewlett-Packard in a garage in Palo Alto. In 1951, Stanford opened an industrial park where new technology companies could build offices. In the 1950s, companies began making tiny electronic parts out of silicon. These parts became the "brains" inside computers and many other machines.

More and more technology companies started in the valley. In 1971, a writer named Don Hoefler made the name "Silicon Valley" popular. Today, the name often means the whole San Francisco Bay Area. Famous companies such as Apple, Google, and Intel are based there.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: People moved to Silicon Valley for opportunity. New companies needed scientists, engineers, and factory workers, and they offered good jobs. In 1956, the company Lockheed opened in Sunnyvale and soon had 28,000 workers. In 1957, William Shockley brought young scientists and engineers from the East Coast to work at his new lab.

In 1965, the United States passed a new immigration law. It gave special priority to skilled workers and professionals. After that, many more immigrants came from Asia and other parts of the world. In the 1960s and 1970s, the growing electronics industry also drew people who wanted to start their own companies.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Newcomers came from all over the United States and from many countries. Immigrants, especially from East and South Asia, came in wave after wave. A study in 1999 found that about one-third of Silicon Valley's scientists and engineers were immigrants. Nearly a quarter of the technology companies started there after 1980 had leaders of Chinese or Indian background.

Most newcomers settled in cities such as San Jose, Palo Alto, Mountain View, Sunnyvale, and Cupertino. San Jose became the largest city in Silicon Valley. Unlike many migrations in history, most of these people chose to move to find a better job.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Silicon Valley changed from a quiet farming valley into a busy center of technology. Orchards were replaced by offices, factories, and neighborhoods. By 2020, about 3.1 million people lived there. Inventions made in Silicon Valley, like computer chips and websites, are now used all over the world.

Growth also brought problems. Homes in Silicon Valley became very expensive, with an average price of about $1 million. Some families with middle incomes have had to move away. Traffic and long drives to work have also been problems for many years.

Newcomers made Silicon Valley a home for people from many different countries. Families from many countries brought their languages, foods, and traditions. Many immigrants started companies that created jobs for others. People keep moving to Silicon Valley today, hoping to build new technology and a new life.

name: Chernobyl
place: Chernobyl and Pripyat, Ukraine (then part of the Soviet Union)
intro: On April 26, 1986, a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine, which was then part of the Soviet Union. It was the worst nuclear accident in history. Dangerous radiation spread over the land, and the whole city of Pripyat and many nearby villages had to be emptied, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to leave their homes for good.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: April 26, 1986

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, near Pripyat in northern Ukraine

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: The people of Pripyat and villages near the power plant

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 49,000 people from Pripyat; about 335,000 people in all

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Nearby towns and villages, and later the new city of Slavutych

timeline.text: The city of Pripyat is founded as a home for workers at the Chernobyl power plant.
At 1:23 a.m., reactor number 4 explodes during a safety test.
More than 1,000 buses carry all of Pripyat's people away in just a few hours.
Scientists in Sweden find radiation in the air, and Soviet leaders admit there was an accident.
The last working reactor at Chernobyl is shut down.
A giant new steel shelter, the New Safe Confinement, is slid over the damaged reactor.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: The Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant made electricity for the Soviet Union. It was in northern Ukraine, which was part of the Soviet Union at the time. Nearby was the city of Pripyat, built in 1970 for the plant's workers and their families. About 49,000 people lived there.

Early in the morning on April 26, 1986, workers ran a safety test on reactor number 4. They broke important safety rules, and the reactor had design problems too. At 1:23 a.m., the reactor suddenly got too hot and exploded. The blast blew the heavy roof off the building and started fires.

The explosion sent radioactive material high into the air. Wind carried it far away, all the way to Sweden. Two workers died in the explosion, and 28 emergency workers died from radiation sickness in the months after. It was the worst nuclear accident in history.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Radiation is a kind of energy you cannot see, smell, or feel. Large amounts of it can make people very sick. After the explosion, the land, water, and buildings near the plant were full of dangerous radiation. People could not safely live there anymore.

At first, Soviet leaders kept the accident a secret. They did not tell the people of Pripyat for about 36 hours. On April 28, scientists in Sweden found radiation in the air and traced it back to the Soviet Union. Only then did Soviet leaders admit there had been an accident.
Officials later emptied every village within about 30 kilometers (19 miles) of the plant. This area became the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. People are still not allowed to live there today.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: On the afternoon of April 27, 1986, soldiers and police came to Pripyat. They used more than 1,000 buses to move all of the city's people in just a few hours. Families were told they would come back in three days. Because of that, most people left almost all of their belongings behind.
The buses took people to towns and villages farther from the plant. In the weeks after, people from many more villages had to leave too. In all, the Soviet Union evacuated about 335,000 people.

The families of Pripyat never went home. The government built a brand-new city called Slavutych just for the people who had lived in Pripyat. They had to start over in a new place, far from the homes they had left.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Pripyat became a ghost town. Today, no one lives there at all. Its empty apartment buildings, schools, and amusement park still stand, just as people left them in 1986.

Workers covered the broken reactor with a concrete and steel shell a few months after the accident. In November 2016, a huge new steel shelter was slid over it to keep the radiation inside. The last working reactor at Chernobyl was shut down in 2000. Cleanup work is expected to last until at least 2065.

With no people around, wild animals moved into the Exclusion Zone. Wolves, wild boars, lynx, elk, and rare Przewalski's horses now roam the empty land. Scientists study the animals to learn how radiation affects living things.

name: Indian Ocean Tsunami (2004)
place: Aceh, Indonesia, and countries around the Indian Ocean
intro: On December 26, 2004, a huge earthquake shook the ocean floor near Sumatra, an island in Indonesia. It sent giant waves called a tsunami across the Indian Ocean. The waves hit 17 countries, and the Aceh province of Indonesia was hit the hardest. About 1.7 million people had to leave their homes.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: December 26, 2004

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Aceh, Indonesia, plus Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and other countries around the Indian Ocean

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Families who lived along the coasts, especially in Aceh

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 1.7 million people were displaced (forced from their homes)

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Temporary shelters and tents, then rebuilt homes and towns

timeline.text: On the morning of December 26, a magnitude 9.1 earthquake struck under the ocean near Sumatra, Indonesia.
Within about 15 to 20 minutes, the first waves reached Banda Aceh, a city in Indonesia.
Over the next hours, the waves crossed the Indian Ocean and reached Thailand, Sri Lanka, India, and even Africa.
Most of the rebuilding work by the aid group World Vision was finished, including thousands of new homes.
Twenty years later, students in Aceh practiced tsunami drills so they would be ready for the future.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: On December 26, 2004, a giant earthquake struck under the Indian Ocean. It happened off the west coast of Sumatra, an island in Indonesia. The earthquake measured 9.1, which makes it one of the strongest earthquakes ever recorded. The shaking lasted for about eight to ten minutes.

The earthquake suddenly moved a huge amount of ocean water. This made a tsunami, a series of giant ocean waves. In deep water, tsunami waves can travel up to 500 miles per hour. In Aceh, Indonesia, the waves reached as high as 167 feet and pushed up to 3 miles inland.

The waves hit 17 countries, from Indonesia and Thailand to Sri Lanka, India, and East Africa. About 230,000 people died or went missing. Indonesia lost the most people, more than 160,000, and most of them lived in Aceh. Many villages along the coasts were washed away.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: The waves destroyed houses, schools, roads, and fishing boats. In Aceh, more than 1,400 schools were wrecked. About 1.7 million people around the Indian Ocean were displaced. That means they were forced to leave their homes because their homes were gone or unsafe.

In 2004, the Indian Ocean had no official tsunami warning system. In Banda Aceh, the first waves came only 15 to 20 minutes after the earthquake. Few people knew that an earthquake could cause a tsunami, so there was little time to run to higher ground.

Salty ocean water also soaked the land. Salty soil is very hard to farm, so many farms were ruined. Fishing and tourism were hurt the most, because many boats and beach areas were destroyed. Many families lost their jobs as well as their homes.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Most survivors did not travel far away. They moved to safer places nearby while their towns were cleaned up and rebuilt. Aid workers gave families tarps to make shelters. Groups also set up Child-Friendly Spaces, where children could play and feel safe.

People and countries around the world sent help. Over 7 billion dollars was donated to rebuild the damaged areas. One aid group, World Vision, built 12,000 homes, 84 schools, and 27 health clinics in the countries that were hit.
Rebuilding took years. Most of World Vision's rebuilding work was done by 2007. Workers also planted 56,000 mangrove trees along the coast. These trees can help slow down big waves in the future.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: The tsunami changed how countries around the Indian Ocean prepare for disasters. After 2004, countries built tsunami warning centers. Australia, India, and Indonesia led this new Indian Ocean warning system. Aceh also set up early warning systems near the shore.

Children in Aceh now learn what to do when the ground shakes. At one high school, students practice a tsunami drill on the 26th of every month. When the alarm sounds, they hide under their tables and then move quickly to a safe meeting place.

People in Aceh still remember the tsunami. A mosque in Lampuuk that was only partly damaged by the waves is now a symbol of remembrance. A huge power ship that the waves carried inland in Banda Aceh is now a place people visit. Twenty years later, the people of Aceh had rebuilt their towns, and many roads and buildings were stronger than before.

name: Hurricane Katrina
place: New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, United States
intro: In August 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. In New Orleans, the walls that held back the water broke, and about 80 percent of the city flooded. More than one million people had to leave their homes, and many New Orleans families started new lives in Houston and other cities.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: August 29, 2005 (the storm hit land)

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: New Orleans, Louisiana, and the Gulf Coast of Mississippi and Alabama

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Families from New Orleans and other Gulf Coast towns

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: More than 1 million people had to leave their homes

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Houston, San Antonio, Baton Rouge, Atlanta, and cities in all 50 states

timeline.text: A storm forms over the Bahamas and grows into Hurricane Katrina.
New Orleans orders everyone to leave the city for the first time ever.
Katrina hits Louisiana and Mississippi. Levees break, and about 80 percent of New Orleans floods.
Thousands of people are taken by bus to shelters in Houston, including the Astrodome.
Only about 230,000 people live in New Orleans, less than half as many as before the storm.
New Orleans has about 390,000 people again, after years of rebuilding and new flood walls.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: Hurricane Katrina formed near the Bahamas on August 23, 2005. Over the warm Gulf of Mexico, it grew into a Category 5 storm with winds of 175 miles per hour. On August 29, it hit southeast Louisiana and Mississippi with winds of about 125 miles per hour. A huge rise of seawater, called a storm surge, flooded the coast.

New Orleans is a city that sits lower than the sea around it. Tall walls called levees were supposed to keep the water out. During Katrina, the levees broke in more than 50 places. Water poured in, and about 80 percent of the city flooded, in some places up to 20 feet deep.
Katrina was one of the deadliest hurricanes in U.S. history. More than 1,800 people died. It was also the costliest hurricane ever to hit the United States, causing more than $100 billion in damage.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: The day before the storm, the mayor ordered everyone to leave New Orleans. About 1.2 million people along the Gulf Coast evacuated, and most people in New Orleans left. But many people could not leave. Some did not have a car or money, and some were old or sick.

About 20,000 people took shelter in the Superdome, a large football stadium. It had no electricity or working bathrooms. After the flood, rescuers saved about 60,000 people from rooftops and flooded streets.
When the water finally drained away, many homes were ruined. Schools, stores, and jobs were gone too. Families could not come back right away because there was no safe place to live.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Starting in early September, buses carried thousands of people from New Orleans to Houston, Texas. Houston opened its giant Astrodome stadium as a shelter. More than 25,000 people lived there for a while, sleeping on cots on the stadium floor.

Many evacuees settled in Houston and decided to stay. Other families moved to San Antonio, Baton Rouge, and Atlanta. Some went to Mobile, Alabama, and others moved even farther away. Katrina families ended up living in all 50 states.

More than one million people had to leave their homes. It was the largest move of people in modern American history. Some families lived in shelters, hotels, or with relatives for months or even years.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Before Katrina, about 485,000 people lived in New Orleans. By 2006, only about 230,000 people lived there. Thousands of people never moved back. Many started new lives in Houston and other cities, where their children grew up and went to school.
Little by little, people rebuilt New Orleans. The government spent about $14 billion to build stronger flood walls, gates, and giant pumps. By 2020, the city had grown back to about 390,000 people.

Katrina also changed how the country gets ready for disasters. Congress said all levels of government must practice working together when a disaster strikes. Today, people who lived through Katrina share their stories so others can learn from them.

vocab.meaning: A huge, powerful storm with very strong winds and heavy rain that forms over warm ocean water.

name: Japan Earthquake and Tsunami (2011)
intro: On March 11, 2011, the strongest earthquake ever recorded in Japan shook the ocean floor near the country's northeast coast. It caused a tsunami that flooded towns along the coast and damaged a nuclear power plant in Fukushima. More than 470,000 people had to leave their homes.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: March 11, 2011, at 2:46 in the afternoon

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: The Tohoku region of northeastern Japan, including Miyagi, Iwate, and Fukushima

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Families from coastal towns and from the area around the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: More than 470,000 people were evacuated from their homes

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Evacuation centers, then temporary housing, and later new permanent homes

timeline.text: On March 11 at 2:46 p.m., a magnitude 9.0 earthquake struck off the northeast coast of Japan.
Within 30 minutes, tsunami waves reached the coast and rushed over the seawalls.
The tsunami knocked out power and cooling at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, and people living within 12 miles had to leave.
In July, Japan's government made a 10-year plan to rebuild the damaged region.
A memorial opened in the city of Ishinomaki to remember the disaster.
About 30,000 people were still living away from their old homes.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: On March 11, 2011, at 2:46 in the afternoon, a huge earthquake struck under the Pacific Ocean. It happened off the northeast coast of Japan, in an area called Tohoku. The earthquake measured 9.0, the largest ever recorded in Japan. The ground shook for about six minutes.

The earthquake caused a tsunami, a series of giant ocean waves. The waves reached the coast in less than 30 minutes and rushed over the seawalls. In some places the water rose almost 130 feet high. Near the city of Sendai, the water flowed up to 6 miles inland.

More than 18,000 people died or were never found. Most of the damage came from the tsunami, not the shaking. More than 123,000 houses were completely destroyed. The waves even crossed the Pacific Ocean and were measured in more than 25 countries.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Many families had to leave because the tsunami destroyed their homes and neighborhoods. Whole towns along the coast were flooded. Millions of homes lost electricity, and more than a million homes lost running water.

The tsunami also damaged the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. The water knocked out the plant's power, so it could not keep three of its reactors cool. The reactors were badly damaged and released radiation, a kind of energy that can make people sick. To keep people safe, the government ordered everyone living within 12 miles (20 kilometers) of the plant to evacuate.
In all, more than 470,000 people were evacuated from their homes. About 165,000 of them were from Fukushima prefecture. Up to 100,000 children were displaced by the disaster.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: At first, many families stayed in evacuation centers. These centers had community kitchens where people could get meals. Aid groups set up Child-Friendly Spaces where children could play and feel safe.

Later, many families moved into temporary housing while their towns were rebuilt. In 2016, about 60,800 people still lived in temporary housing. By 2018, about 92 percent of the planned new public housing was finished.

Some people could not go home for many years. Families from near the nuclear plant waited until it was safe to return. The government cleaned up towns and lifted evacuation orders in almost all areas. But a small area close to the plant was still closed, called a "difficult-to-return" area.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: In July 2011, Japan's government made a 10-year plan to rebuild. Workers cleared the debris and rebuilt most of the roads, bridges, railways, and airports. Towns built new seawalls and made better plans to help people evacuate.
The number of evacuees went down year by year as people moved into new homes. By May 2023, about 30,000 people were still evacuees. Only about 1,000 of them were still in temporary housing.

Scientists studied the tsunami to learn how to keep people safer. They collected more than 6,400 measurements of the waves. Warning systems helped save many lives, both in Japan and across the Pacific Ocean. In 2016, a memorial opened in the city of Ishinomaki so people can remember those who were lost.

name: Nepal Earthquake (2015)
intro: On April 25, 2015, a powerful earthquake struck the mountain country of Nepal. It destroyed villages, homes, schools, and famous old temples. About 9,000 people died, and millions of people lost their homes.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: April 25, 2015, with a second big earthquake on May 12, 2015

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Central Nepal, near the Gorkha District and the capital city, Kathmandu

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Families in mountain villages and cities whose homes were destroyed

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 2.6 million people had to move from their communities

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Tents and temporary shelters near their villages, then rebuilt homes

timeline.text: On April 25 at 11:56 a.m., a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck near the Gorkha District of Nepal.
The shaking knocked down the Dharahara tower and old temples in Kathmandu and set off an avalanche on Mount Everest.
On May 12, a second strong earthquake, measuring 7.3, struck Nepal.
About five weeks after the first earthquake, 14,000 children went back to school in temporary classrooms.
In December, Nepal set up a national agency to lead the rebuilding.
On September 19, a newly rebuilt Dharahara tower opened to visitors in Kathmandu.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: On April 25, 2015, just before noon, a strong earthquake shook Nepal. Nepal is a small country in the Himalaya Mountains, between India and China. The earthquake measured 7.8. It started near the Gorkha District, about 50 miles northwest of the capital city, Kathmandu.

The shaking lasted about 50 seconds, but it caused huge damage. Homes, schools, roads, and bridges fell apart. In Kathmandu, the tall Dharahara tower, built in 1832, collapsed. Several old temples in Kathmandu Durbar Square also fell down.

About 9,000 people died, and about 22,000 people were hurt. The shaking also caused an avalanche on Mount Everest. Then, on May 12, a second strong earthquake measuring 7.3 hit Nepal and caused even more damage.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Millions of people lost their homes in the earthquakes. In one village, all 25 houses were destroyed. About 2.6 million people had to move away from their communities.

Aftershocks, smaller earthquakes that come after a big one, kept shaking the ground. By May 2016, Nepal had felt 459 aftershocks of magnitude 4 or higher. During strong aftershocks, people hurried to open spaces away from buildings.
Schools were hit hard too. More than half of Nepal's schools were damaged or destroyed. Close to 1 million children could not go to school.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Most families did not travel far. They stayed close to their villages and lived in tents and temporary shelters. Nearly 1.7 million children were living outdoors after the earthquake. UNICEF and other groups handed out tents, clean water, and hygiene kits.

Getting help to mountain villages was hard. Many villages could only be reached by dirt roads or footpaths. When the monsoon rains began in June, landslides blocked the paths. Low clouds also kept helicopters from flying.

Nepal's army and many other countries helped with rescue work. Groups built temporary classrooms out of bamboo poles covered with tarps. About five weeks after the first earthquake, 14,000 children were back at school in 137 of these learning centers. Going to school gave children a safe place and a normal daily routine.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Rebuilding Nepal took many years. In December 2015, the government set up a national agency to lead the work. Even in 2016, about 70 percent of people who had lost their homes were still living in temporary shelters. Rebuilding continued through 2017 and 2018.

Countries around the world promised about 3 billion dollars to help Nepal. A special program helped families in the hardest-hit areas rebuild their houses. Aid groups also rebuilt schools and repaired water systems for farms.

Nepal also worked to rebuild its famous landmarks. A new Dharahara tower was built in Kathmandu. It opened to visitors on September 19, 2024, nine years after the old tower fell. The new tower has 22 floors, a museum, and a garden.

vocab.meaning: A sudden shaking of the ground caused by rocks moving deep under the Earth's surface.
A number that tells how strong an earthquake is. Bigger numbers mean stronger earthquakes.
A smaller earthquake that happens after a big earthquake in the same area.
A large amount of snow and ice that suddenly slides down a mountain.

name: The Camp Fire (2018)
intro: On November 8, 2018, a wildfire called the Camp Fire started in the hills of Northern California. Strong winds pushed it into the town of Paradise, and in less than a day it destroyed most of the town. It was the deadliest wildfire in California history, and thousands of families had to find new homes.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: November 8–25, 2018

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Paradise, Concow, and Magalia in Butte County, California

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Families from Paradise and nearby towns

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 26,000 people lived in Paradise; by 2020, fewer than 5,000 lived there

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Chico and other nearby towns, and cities such as Boise, Denver, Salt Lake City, and Crossville, Tennessee

timeline.text: Around 6:30 in the morning, a fire starts near Camp Creek Road in Butte County.
Strong winds push the fire into Paradise. The whole town is told to leave.
With help from three days of rain, firefighters fully contain the fire.
The town gives out its first two permits to rebuild homes.
The census counts 4,764 people in Paradise, down from about 26,000 before the fire.
More than 9,000 people live in Paradise, and over 2,500 new buildings have gone up.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: Early on the morning of November 8, 2018, a fire started in a canyon in Butte County, California. The area is about 90 miles north of Sacramento. The land was very dry because it had not rained much for about 200 days. The fire was started by equipment that belonged to a power company.

Strong winds blew the fire toward the town of Paradise, about 7 miles away. Burning bits of plants flew ahead of the flames and started new fires. In less than 24 hours, the fire swept through Paradise and the nearby towns of Concow and Magalia.

The Camp Fire burned for more than two weeks and covered about 240 square miles. It destroyed more than 18,000 buildings, including nearly 14,000 homes. Sadly, 85 people died. It was the deadliest and most destructive wildfire in California history.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Officials first told people in eastern Paradise to leave. About an hour later, they told the whole town to go. Many people did not get a warning, or they did not understand how serious the fire was. Thousands of people tried to drive out of town at the same time.

The roads out of town became jammed with traffic. Fallen power lines and burning plants blocked some roads. The fire chief told firefighters to stop fighting the fire and focus on one job: helping people escape.

When the fire was over, almost nothing was left of Paradise. Only about 5 out of every 100 buildings in town were not badly damaged. Families had no house to go back to, and schools, stores, and jobs were gone too.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Many families moved to Chico, the closest city. But Chico did not have enough homes for everyone who needed one. Families with more money had an easier time finding a place to live there.

Other families moved much farther away. Small groups settled in cities like Boise, Idaho; Denver, Colorado; Salt Lake City, Utah; and Orlando, Florida. Some even moved to the small town of Crossville, Tennessee. Half of the people age 65 and older moved more than 30 miles away from the fire.
Many other families stayed in the area and kept a mailbox at the Paradise post office. Before the fire, about 26,000 people lived in Paradise. By April 2019, only about 2,000 people lived there.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Rebuilding Paradise took a long time. Workers first had to clear away the burned buildings. The first two permits to build new homes were given out on March 28, 2019, almost five months after the fire.

Town leaders wanted Paradise to be safer from fire. They asked for buildings that resist fire and better roads for leaving in an emergency. Little by little, people came home and new families moved in.
By November 2023, more than 9,000 people lived in Paradise. More than 2,500 new buildings had been built. Many families who left never came back, but Paradise is slowly growing again.

vocab.meaning: A large fire that spreads quickly through forests, grass, or brush.
To leave a dangerous place to get to safety.
A long time with little or no rain.
For a fire, to stop it from spreading any farther.
A paper from the government that says you are allowed to do something, like build a house.

name: Russia–Ukraine War
intro: On February 24, 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine, and a full-scale war began. Millions of Ukrainian families left their homes to find safety, either in other parts of Ukraine or in other countries. As of February 2026, the United Nations counted nearly 6 million refugees from Ukraine around the world.

keyFacts.label: When
keyFacts.value: February 24, 2022, to today

keyFacts.label: Where
keyFacts.value: Ukraine, and neighboring countries such as Poland, Moldova, Romania, Slovakia, and Hungary

keyFacts.label: Who moved
keyFacts.value: Ukrainian families, most of them women and children

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: 5,923,870 refugees from Ukraine recorded around the world, and about 3.7 million people displaced inside Ukraine, as of February 19, 2026 (UNHCR)

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Safer parts of Ukraine, and countries across Europe, about 5.3 million of them

timeline.text: Conflict between Russia and Ukraine begins, with fighting in eastern Ukraine.
On February 24, Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
By March 3, more than one million people have fled Ukraine to neighboring countries.
UNICEF and its partners reach 2.5 million children in Ukraine with help such as safe water, health care, and schooling.
In February, as the war enters its fifth year, nearly 2.6 million Ukrainian children are still away from their homes.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: Ukraine is a large country in Eastern Europe, next to Russia. Fighting between the two countries began in eastern Ukraine in 2014. Then, on February 24, 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine with a much larger attack. This started a full-scale war that is still going on.

The war has caused great harm to people in Ukraine. Attacks have damaged homes, power plants, and water systems in many cities. More than 1,700 schools and other places of learning have been damaged or destroyed. The United Nations has recorded more than 14,000 civilians, or people who are not soldiers, killed since 2022.

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: People left their homes to stay safe from the fighting. In a UNICEF survey, safety was the most common reason young people gave for fleeing. Many families also lost their homes, or had no electricity, heat, or clean water. Some families had to move more than once as the fighting moved closer.

Most of the people who left Ukraine were women and children. In Poland, about 8 out of every 10 refugees were women and children. A chef who helped refugees at the border said people carried only what they could bring. Many hoped to return home when it was safe again.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: In the first days of the war, crowds of people waited at train stations in Kyiv, Ukraine's capital. Families traveled by train and bus to reach the borders. By March 3, 2022, more than one million people had already left Ukraine. Many crossed into Poland, where volunteers handed out hot meals at the border.

As of February 19, 2026, the United Nations counted 5,923,870 refugees from Ukraine around the world. About 5.3 million of them were living in countries across Europe. Neighboring countries such as Poland, Moldova, Romania, Slovakia, and Hungary took in many refugees. Another 3.7 million people moved to safer places inside Ukraine.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: The war changed life for millions of Ukrainian children. As of February 2026, UNICEF said nearly 2.6 million children were still displaced from their homes. About 1.8 million of them were living as refugees in other countries. About one in three children inside Ukraine could not go to school in person full-time.

Refugee children had to start over in new countries, often in new schools and with a new language. Countries in Europe let Ukrainian refugees stay and get help through special protection programs. UNICEF helped refugee children join local schools and gave families health care, safe water, and money for basic needs.

Many people around the world have worked to help. Inside Ukraine, UNICEF repaired schools and water systems and gave families warm clothes and blankets for winter. About one million refugees and displaced people have returned home, but many places are still not safe. Ukrainian families continue to show courage as they wait for peace.

vocab.meaning: A person who has to leave their country to escape war or danger.
Forced to leave your home and live somewhere else.
To send an army into another country to attack or take it over.
A person who is not a soldier.
The line where one country ends and another country begins.
Help such as food, water, shelter, and medicine given to people in a crisis.

teacherNote: This is an ongoing war, and some students may have personal or family connections to Ukraine or Russia. The page stays neutral, focuses on refugee families, and mentions the civilian death toll once without detail. Numbers are given "as of" the date stated by UNHCR or UNICEF and will change.
